Spain Train Collision
A high-speed train
rear-ended another
about 100 miles south of Madrid yesterday, killing at least 68 people and injuring over 60 others (
see photos
, warning—sensitive). The accident occurred nine months after a collision involving the same operators and rail line resulted in 46 deaths.
At around 8:30 am local time, a security system covering approximately 39 miles of tracks on the Madrid-Seville line failed due to a computer malfunction. Six trains stopped as a precaution until Spain’s central command center authorized a southbound train to proceed. It traveled roughly 16 miles at around 124 mph before crashing into a stationary train. The collision sent carriages from each down an embankment (
watch aerial footage
Travel via train accounts for around 57% of Spain’s transport, and over 90% of its network features the highest level of safety control systems in the EU. The country boasts over 2,400 miles of high-speed track, second only to China. See where the US ranks in high-speed rail length
here
Bolsonaro Arrives Stateside
Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family
landed in Miami yesterday
(w/photos) after fleeing Brazil and obtaining visas from the Trump administration. See flight path
here
The nationalist-populist senator has yet to concede Sunday’s presidential runoff to leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, as the official tally recorded a loss by 4.4 million votes. After the results were announced, Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passport amid ongoing criminal investigations. The court, which critics say favors the political left, accuses Bolsonaro of laundering money stolen from senior citizens and fraudulently raising money for a biopic about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro (
watch leaked trailer
). The elder Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after narrowly losing Brazil's 2022 election.
President Donald Trump has suggested this weekend's
election was "rigged,"
without citing evidence. He was a close ally of the elder Bolsonaro and imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian imports last year in retaliation for his prosecution.
How Does a 392-Degree Day Sound?
Unless you're named Barbie or Ken, you won’t survive. At 392°F, plastic is one of the only things left standing. And since
3D printers
run at that temp to manipulate printing materials, that limits their output to practically one thing: plastic.
Until
String Cubed
, that is. They invented a way to build water into printing materials to carry heat away. That allows anything from soap to vitamins and proteins to survive the 3D printers’ previously destructive heat. What that unlocks is
enormous
. Imagine a future where an at-home device
prints food, medicine, structural materials, and anything else
that once needed factories.
And they hold the only patent in the field. They’re already printing and selling multiple distinct products, from self-watering seed pods to shrimp protein.

World Series Winners
The Milwaukee Brewers
clinched their first World Series
in franchise history yesterday, defeating Tampa Bay 4-1 at the Rays’ home field in St. Petersburg, Florida. Watch the final out
here
(via X).
Milwaukee appeared poised for a sweep through the first three matchups. In Game 3, the Brewers
set a World Series record
by scoring eight two-out runs in a single inning. That offensive explosion resulted in a 10-1 victory, the largest World Series run differential since 2019. But Tampa Bay clawed out a 4-3 win in 12 innings in Game 4 to avoid the sweep. Milwaukee bounced back last night, powered by starting pitcher
Jacob Misiorowski
, left fielder
Jackson Chourio
, infielder
Cooper Pratt
, and others. Brewers catcher
William Contreras
was named MVP after hitting .381 with four RBIs in the series.
In addition to the Commissioner's Trophy, Milwaukee will get a Monet painting through a loan from St. Petersburg’s Museum of Fine Arts. The art directors of the cities’ museums
wagered pieces
from their collections on the Fall Classic.

Turning Star Trek Into Standard Tech
In Star Trek, machines conjured anything from medicine to a cup of tea.
3D printing
wishes it could be that versatile. Instead, it mostly prints things made of plastic.
Why? Printers run at 392°F, destroying almost anything
but
plastic. So
String Cubed
invented a way to protect delicate materials at high temps, opening new doors for 3D printing. Now, they’re building “The Manifester” to print food, medicine, and anything else on demand. Sound familiar?
